points.text: Composition: the Layout section holds a mat, a text position and a shape for the map. The three together decide how the poster sits on the paper.
The mat is a border in the background color. The map keeps your location at the center of the hole, so the poster still shows the place you chose.
Four shapes for the map: Full, Rounded, Circle and Arch.
The gradient fades of the “Overlay layer” switch follow the map now, not the paper. A shape turns them off, so a circle keeps a clean edge.
The poster text has one control again. It sits in the Composition block, and the “Poster text” switch in the Style section is gone.
A slider sets the width of the mat, from 0 to 20 percent of the short side of the poster.
The edge that carries the text takes a wider border, so the text can move off the map and onto the mat. This is the classic print: the map above, the name below.
The mat takes the background color of the theme, so every theme brings its own paper.
The text block sits at the bottom, at the top, or nowhere. The city, the country and the coordinates move together.
This is the only control for the poster text now. The Style section no longer carries a switch of its own, and “None” gives the map the space the text used.
The shape cuts the map: Full keeps the rectangle, Rounded softens the corners, Circle cuts a disc and Arch cuts a window.
A link carries the composition. The keys are mat, text and mask, and each one appears only when it differs from the default.
The “Overlay layer” switch works as before: it fades the top and the bottom of the map into the paper. With a mat the fades sit at the edge of the map, not at the edge of the sheet.
The PNG, the PDF and the SVG all read the same composition as the preview, so the file repeats what you saw.
The SVG carries the mat as one vector shape, not as a picture. An editor can recolor it.
A marker keeps its place under a mat. It sits on the same point in the preview, in the PNG and in the SVG.
Presets: named starting points that set the theme, the drawing, the composition and the layers at once.
Caption lines and a frame line join the composition later.
Export resolution: the download dialog asks how many pixels you want. A print poster offers 150, 200 and 300 DPI. A wallpaper offers its named size and twice that size.
A readout names the result before you export, for example "A2 - 4961 x 7016 px - about 35 MB". The file you receive matches it.
A PNG carries its real resolution now. A large poster used to claim 300 DPI and open at the wrong size in a print shop.
A poster reaches 120 cm now, so A2, A1 and A0 fit.
Print sizes: 150, 200 and 300 DPI. An A2 poster at 300 DPI holds 4961 x 7016 pixels. It used to leave the app at 2450 x 3466, which is 148 DPI on that paper.
Pixel sizes: a wallpaper, a social post and a web image export at their named size. A 4K wallpaper is 3840 x 2160 pixels now, not 3543 x 1993. The 2x option doubles it for a high-density screen.
Standard is the resolution of release 0.7. It stays on the list, and it stays the answer where a device cannot hold more.
The choice stays on this device. It is not part of a link, because it describes your machine and not your design.
The readout sits under the picker and under the size fields in the Layout section. It names the pixel size and the size of the file.
The PNG header carries the real resolution: pixels divided by inches. A print shop opens the file at the size it really holds.
The PDF keeps the page size in centimeters and holds the whole image, so a higher resolution raises the detail of the print.
The layered SVG keeps the standard resolution. It embeds one image per map layer, about twenty five of them, and a higher resolution would make the file very large.
The app asks your browser for the graphics limit and the memory of the machine, and it suggests 300 DPI where they allow it.
An option above that limit stays on the list and carries the words "may fail on this device". You keep the choice.
An export that does not fit stops with a clear message and the dialog stays open. You never receive a file that differs from the readout.
Composition: a mat, the text position and a mask for the map follow in the next release.
Presets: named starting points that set the theme, the drawing, the composition and the layers at once.
Relief: the Layers section draws the terrain. Contour lines and a hillshade each have their own switch.
Contour interval: you choose Auto, 10, 20, 50 or 100 meters. The hillshade has two strengths, Soft and Strong.
The export reports what it does: it names the phase, and it stops with a clear message when a tile fails to load.
Relief is off until you turn it on. The default poster does not change.
Contour lines: the map draws the height lines of the land. The interval is Auto, or a fixed 10, 20, 50 or 100 meters. Every fifth line is a heavier major line.
Hillshade: the light of a low sun models the slopes. Soft keeps the map flat and calm. Strong pushes the mountains forward.
Every theme: the contour lines take the text color and the hillshade takes tones of the land color, so relief works with all 29 themes.
Every export follows: the PNG, the PDF and the layered SVG all carry the relief. In the SVG, the hillshade and the two contour layers are their own layer groups.

The data are Tilezen terrain tiles. Your browser loads them from Amazon Web Services while a relief switch is on, and sends nothing to Amazon while both switches are off. The full credit sits in the map attribution dialog in the footer.
Phases: the download dialog reports Loading terrain, Rendering map and Building file. Real map events drive the text.
No more holes: a poster used to export with a blank area when a map tile failed to load. The export now stops and says so.
The dialog stays open when an export stops, and it shows the reason.
The address bar holds the relief values. A link restores the contour interval and the hillshade strength.
Old links still work. A link without the new keys opens a poster without relief.
Composition: a mat, the text position and a mask for the map follow in the next release.
Presets: named starting points that set the theme, the drawing, the composition and the layers at once.
The plate: three controls in the Layers section change how the map draws. You set the line weight, you draw the areas as outlines, and you remove the road casings.
Three named plates: Full, Line and Bold set all three drawing rules with one click.
The link carries the drawing: a permalink now holds the plate values and the layers that you switched off.
The default poster does not change. The app opens with the Full plate, which draws the poster of release 0.5.

steps.title: The plate: how the map draws

points.text: Line weight: one slider multiplies every line width on the map, from one half to two times.
Outline fills: water, parks, landcover and buildings draw as their border only. The border keeps the color of the area, moved towards the text color, so that a thin line stays visible.
Road casings: the light halo under the roads has its own switch.
Named plates: Full is the drawing of release 0.5. Line draws outlines and no casings. Bold keeps the fills and makes the lines heavier.
One click, then free: a named plate sets the three rules. Every rule stays editable on its own afterwards.
Drawing, not content: the plate changes how the map draws. The switches above it stay the content of the map.
Every export follows: the PNG, the PDF and the layered SVG all use the plate. In the SVG, each outline is its own layer group.
The address bar holds the plate values and the list of the layers that you switched off.
Short links: a key appears in the link only when its value differs from the default.
Old links still work. A link without the new keys opens the default drawing.
Relief: contour lines and hillshade join the Layers section in the next release.
Composition: a mat, the text position and a mask for the map follow after that.
Eight new themes: Catppuccin Mocha, Nord, Dracula, Gruvbox, Tokyo Night, Iris, Glacier and Bauhaus join the list. Each one paints the buildings in three tones by height.
Poster credits switch: the Style section can remove the credit lines from the poster.
New look: the interface uses slate surfaces and one gold accent, both taken from the logo. The panels are flat.
Theme cards: the Classic and Candy cards now show their building colors. Before this fix, three of their five columns stayed empty.
Popular palettes: Catppuccin Mocha, Nord, Dracula, Gruvbox and Tokyo Night follow the editor palettes of the same names. All five palettes are MIT licensed.
Three originals: Iris (lilac to indigo), Glacier (ice to navy) and Bauhaus (yellow, red, blue) are light themes made for this site.
Height tones: every new theme paints the buildings in three tones. The map selects the tone from the building height, with the same rule as Classic and Candy.
Theme cards: a card shows the text color, the land color and the three building tones. Classic and Candy showed two colors before this fix.
List order: the ten Erratic themes come first, then the themes from the Terraink base.
Poster credits: a switch in the Style section removes both credit lines from the poster, the OpenStreetMap line and the site line.
Default: the switch is on, so a poster carries its credit unless you decide otherwise.
Your duty: the site keeps its attribution in the footer. If you publish a poster without the credit line, add "© OpenStreetMap contributors" next to it.
Gold on slate: the colors of the interface come from the logo. The surfaces are slate, and the one accent is gold.
Flat panels: the glass blur and the glow shadows are gone. A thin line separates the panels.
One accent: the active tab, the switches, the selected cards and the Download button share the gold.
Unchanged: the layout, the typefaces and the motion stay as they were.
Tokens: every interface color is a variable in one file, so a later change of the palette is small.
New name: Terraink becomes Erratic Maps, with a new logo and a new home at maps.erraticl.uk.
Two new themes: Classic and Candy join the theme list, and the buildings take three tones by height.
Permalinks: the address bar always holds a link to the poster that you see.
No popup after an export: the download ends, and nothing asks you to follow an account.
No trackers: this deployment runs no analytics and no ads.

steps.title: A new name and a new mark

points.text: New name: the fork of Terraink becomes Erratic Maps at maps.erraticl.uk.
New logo: a slate map pin holds a faceted glacial-erratic boulder. Every icon, the map marker and the social banner come from that one drawing.
Credit: the footer names Terraink as the source of the code, as the upstream trademark policy asks.
Saved settings: the new name changed the storage keys, so the app opens with the default settings one time.

steps.title: Two themes and a new building fill

points.text: Classic and Candy: two themes come from the retired predecessor app.
Height triad: a theme can paint the buildings in three tones. The map selects the tone from the building height: under 10 m, 10 m to 24 m, and 24 m or taller.
Why the height: a tile at a low zoom joins a block into one shape. The height is equal on both sides of a tile seam, so a color does not split a building.
New defaults: the poster opens with the Classic theme, and the buildings layer starts visible.
Your color wins: if you select a building color yourself, the app uses that one color and stops the three tones.

steps.title: Share a poster with a link

points.text: Permalinks: the URL holds the location, the distance, the theme, the layout, the custom size and the display names.
Clean history: the app replaces the URL instead of adding a new entry, so the back button still leaves the app.
Pasted links: a permalink that you paste into a running app now applies immediately. Before this fix it needed a manual refresh.
Follow popup: the window that asked you to follow an account after a download is gone.
Blank page after a deploy: the app reloads itself one time when a new deploy hides a code file. A flag stops a reload loop.
Vector icons: the icons in this window are vector drawings instead of emoji.
No analytics: this deployment removes the analytics scripts and the consent banner, because it collects nothing.
Privacy policy: the policy is live, and it describes the real behavior of the site.
Automatic deploy: a GitHub Action builds the site and publishes it on every push to the main branch.
Legal notice: the German imprint waits for a postal address. It goes live after that.

steps.title: Carried over from the Terraink base

points.text: Shared base: Erratic Maps builds on the Terraink source code, under the AGPL-3.0 license.
GPX routes: you can upload a track, draw it on the poster, and set a start marker and a finish marker.
Faster map: the map no longer requests the same tile more than one time.
Local typefaces: the fonts ship with the site instead of coming from a font service.
Response headers: the site sends X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy.
Contributors: the Terraink community added the font style in the dropdown, and the keyboard keys that move a marker.
Terraink release: this version comes from the Terraink project, before the fork.
Marker editing: the marker controls are easier to use.
Xteink X4: the layout list gets the format of that e-ink display.
Location retry: the app tries again when the first request for your position fails.
Lazy loading: the app loads the large parts only when you open them.
Install prompt: the prompt and the service worker work correctly, and the text is clearer.

steps.title: A new interface and Android install

points.text: Terraink release: this version comes from the Terraink project, before the fork.
Android install: you can install the app on an Android device.
Startup location: a dialog asks for the location when the app opens.
Marker size: you can change the marker size with two fingers, with the mouse, or with the minus and plus keys.
New panels: the theme, layout and marker sections get a new design, and the mobile view matches the desktop view.
Docker image: the nginx base image moves to 1.29-alpine and closes 45 known vulnerabilities.
Legal documents: the project adds a trademark policy and a contributor license agreement.

steps.title: Markers, SVG export and this window

points.text: Terraink release: this version comes from the Terraink project, before the fork.
Markers: you can put markers on the map, move them, and change their style.
SVG export: the poster exports as an SVG file with layers.
Map layers: you can switch single map layers on and off.
My location: one button moves the map to your position.
Announcements: this window appears after an update, and it lists the changes.
Print quality: the export uses 300 dots per inch, and the color picker is easier to use.
Terraink release: this version comes from the Terraink project, before the fork.
Live preview: the poster preview becomes an interactive MapLibre map. You can move it and zoom it directly.
PDF export: the poster exports as a PDF file.
Install prompt: you can install the app on your device as a progressive web app.
Rotation: a slider turns the map, and you can set the location from coordinates.
Equal result: the export matches the preview that you see.
New structure: the code moves to TypeScript and to a feature-based architecture.
Terraink release: this is the first version of the project that Erratic Maps forks.
Map posters: the app turns OpenStreetMap data into a poster that you can print.
Themes: the first version ships ten themes, among them Midnight Blue, Blueprint, Forest and Japanese Ink.
PNG export: the app draws the poster on a canvas and saves it as an image.
Origin: the project is a JavaScript reimplementation. The MapToPoster project of Ankur Gupta is its model.
